lead: Angular momentum is the rotational version of linear momentum. For a rigid body it combines the mass moment of inertia with the angular velocity. A moment acting for some time gives an angular impulse, and that impulse changes the body's angular momentum. This idea explains how a brake stops a flywheel, how a clutch brings two shafts to the same speed, and why a coasting rotor keeps its spin. It also gives a quick method for problems where forces and times are known but angular accelerations are awkward to find. The same equation works for fixed-axis rotation and for the rotation part of plane motion.
prereq: You need 6.5 for M = Iα, Unit 4 for mass moment of inertia, and Unit 5 for impulse and momentum.

sections.h3: Angular momentum of a rigid body

blocks.text: For plane motion, let ω be the angular velocity of the body in rad/s. Let I_G be the mass moment of inertia about an axis through the mass centre G, perpendicular to the plane of motion, in kg·m². The angular momentum about G is H_G = I_G ω. H_G is in kg·m²/s, and its sense follows the right-hand rule: curl the fingers in the direction of rotation, the thumb points along H_G. In a plane problem we often use a signed scalar; counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative.
H_G = I_G ω,   H_O = I_O ω
blocks.where: H_G is angular momentum about the mass centre G in kg·m²/s; I_G is the mass moment of inertia about G in kg·m²; ω is angular velocity in rad/s; H_O and I_O refer to a fixed axis through O, perpendicular to the plane.

blocks.text: For a body rotating about a fixed axis through O, perpendicular to the plane, H_O = I_O ω. Here I_O is the mass moment of inertia about that fixed axis. This simple form is special to fixed-axis rotation. In general plane motion, H about a point that is not G also contains a term from the translation of G, so do not replace I_O by I_G blindly.

Why use H? Linear momentum p = m v measures translation; H measures rotation. A heavy flywheel with large I_G stores a large H at modest ω. A small motor rotor has small I_G, so it changes speed quickly. The quantity also tells the direction of spin: reversing ω reverses H.

A moment M about an axis acts for a time. Its angular impulse about that axis is J_θ = ∫ M dt. The unit is N·m·s, which is the same as kg·m²/s. For a constant moment, J_θ = M t. Angular impulse is not a force times a distance; it is a moment times a time.

blocks.where: H₂ and H₁ are angular momenta about the chosen axis in kg·m²/s; M is the external moment about that axis in N·m; t is time in s; ∫ M dt is the angular impulse in N·m·s.

blocks.text: Start from M = Iα = I dω/dt and integrate from time t₁ to t₂. The result is I(ω₂ − ω₁) = ∫ M dt, or H₂ − H₁ = ∫ M dt. This is the angular impulse-momentum relation. Some syllabi call it the moment-of-momentum relation. Choose a positive sense first. A brake opposes rotation, so its moment and its angular impulse are negative when the initial spin is positive.

If the external moment about an axis is zero, then ∫ M dt = 0 about that axis. The angular impulse-momentum relation gives H₂ = H₁. Angular momentum about that axis is conserved. Internal forces and internal moments cancel in pairs, so they cannot change the total H of the system.

A coasting flywheel keeps H constant if bearing friction is negligible. A skater who pulls the arms in changes I and therefore ω, while H stays constant because the external moment about the vertical axis is small. In a clutch, internal friction changes the H of each plate, but the total H of both plates is conserved about the shaft axis.

Conservation holds about the chosen axis, not automatically about every point. A force whose line passes through the axis gives no moment about that axis, so it can change linear momentum while leaving H unchanged. In eccentric impact, the impact force may not pass through G; its moment about G gives an angular impulse and changes H_G. A full 3D treatment needs the inertia tensor and Euler's equations because H is not generally parallel to ω.

figure.caption: A moment gives angular impulse; the impulse equals the change in angular momentum. With no moment about the axis, angular momentum stays constant.

spec.title: Angular impulse
spec.aria: A moment produces angular impulse, which changes angular momentum; if the moment is zero, angular momentum stays constant.

examples.question: A flywheel has mass moment of inertia I = 5.0 kg·m² about its axis and spins at 20 rad/s. A brake applies a constant opposing moment of 10 N·m. Find the time to stop and the angular impulse of the brake.
steps: Take the initial direction of spin as positive. Then ω₁ = 20 rad/s, ω₂ = 0 rad/s, I = 5.0 kg·m², and the brake moment is M = −10 N·m.
Initial angular momentum: H₁ = Iω₁ = 5.0 × 20 = 100 kg·m²/s.
Final angular momentum: H₂ = Iω₂ = 5.0 × 0 = 0 kg·m²/s.
Change in angular momentum: H₂ − H₁ = 0 − 100 = −100 kg·m²/s.
For a constant moment, the angular impulse is M t. So −100 = (−10)t, which gives t = 10 s.
Angular impulse of the brake: ∫M dt = M t = (−10)(10) = −100 N·m·s. Its magnitude is 100 N·m·s, opposite to the spin.
examples.answer: The flywheel stops in 10 s, and the brake's angular impulse has magnitude 100 N·m·s opposing the spin.
examples.check:
I = 5.0
w1 = 20.0
w2 = 0.0
M = 10.0
H1 = I * w1
H2 = I * w2
delta = H2 - H1
t = delta / (-M)
impulse = M * t
print(t)
print(impulse)

traps: Using H = Iω with I taken about a point that is neither the mass centre G nor a point on the fixed rotation axis. In fixed-axis rotation, I about any point on the axis (not only G) is allowed; in general plane motion, H about a point off the axis also needs the r × m v_G term.
Losing the sign of M or angular impulse. A brake opposes rotation, so ΔH and ∫M dt are negative if the initial spin is positive.
Feeding rpm into Iω. Convert ω to rad/s first: ω = 2πN/60 for N in rpm.
Thinking zero external force means H is conserved. H about an axis needs zero external moment about that axis; a force through the axis changes linear momentum but not H about that axis.
Confusing angular impulse ∫M dt with moment M. The impulse depends on how long the moment acts.

quiz.q: State the angular momentum of a rigid body in plane motion about its mass centre.
quiz.a: H_G = I_G ω, where I_G is the mass moment of inertia about G and ω is the angular velocity in rad/s.

quiz.q: Why is angular momentum conserved when the external moment about an axis is zero?
quiz.a: Angular impulse about that axis is ∫M dt = 0, so H₂ − H₁ = 0 and H stays constant; internal moments cancel.

quiz.q: A wheel has I = 2.0 kg·m² about its axis and spins at 15 rad/s. A constant brake moment of 6.0 N·m opposes the spin. Find the stopping time and the brake's angular impulse magnitude.
quiz.a: H₁ = 2.0 × 15 = 30 kg·m²/s; ΔH = −30 kg·m²/s; −6.0t = −30 gives t = 5.0 s; impulse magnitude = 6.0 × 5.0 = 30 N·m·s.

quiz.q: Two coaxial disks, each I = 3.0 kg·m², spin at 12 rad/s and 0 rad/s. They are pressed together and reach a common speed. Which quantity is conserved about the axis and why?
quiz.a: H is conserved if no external moment about the axis acts; internal friction changes each disk's H but total H stays constant. Kinetic energy is not conserved.

quiz.q: Give the SI unit of angular impulse.
A fixed-axis rotor has I_O = 4.0 kg·m² and ω₁ = 10 rad/s. A constant moment of 8.0 N·m acts in the direction of spin for 3.0 s. Find ω₂.
Why is H_O = I_O ω valid for fixed-axis rotation but not for an arbitrary point in general plane motion?
quiz.a: For fixed-axis rotation every point rotates about O with the same ω and O is on the axis. For an arbitrary point, the motion of G adds a translational term to H about that point.

beyond: Not for the exam. In three dimensions the angular momentum vector is not generally parallel to ω, so a body needs the inertia tensor and Euler's equations to predict free rotation. This matters for satellites, gyroscopes and reaction wheels. Vehicle yaw and drone attitude control are everyday users of the same conservation law. Search terms: inertia tensor, Euler equations, gyroscopic couple, reaction wheel.
